clinicalPearls: Occurs with a hypermature or mature cataract, typically in an elderly patient with long-standing poor vision in the affected eye.
Presents acutely with a very high intraocular pressure, pain, redness and corneal oedema, mimicking acute angle closure despite an open angle.
The anterior chamber shows a characteristic pseudohypopyon or iridescent, floating particles representing macrophages laden with lens protein and calcium oxalate crystals.
Gonioscopy reveals an open angle, distinguishing it from angle-closure glaucoma.
Unlike phacoanaphylactic (lens-induced uveitic) glaucoma, the inflammation is a macrophage response to soluble high-molecular-weight lens proteins rather than a granulomatous reaction.
Aqueous aspirate cytology shows swollen macrophages engorged with eosinophilic lens material.
Definitive treatment is prompt cataract extraction after medical control of pressure and inflammation.
Delay risks permanent optic nerve damage from sustained high pressure, so surgery should not be unduly postponed.
reference.pathophysiology: In a hypermature or morgagnian cataract the lens capsule becomes permeable, and soluble high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through microscopic capsular defects into the aqueous humour. These proteins, together with macrophages that engulf them, physically obstruct the trabecular meshwork. The engorged macrophages and the liberated protein and calcium oxalate material clog outflow channels, and the sheer volume of high-molecular-weight protein directly impedes aqueous drainage. Because the angle remains anatomically open, the obstruction is at the level of the meshwork rather than from iridocorneal apposition. The rapid rise in intraocular pressure produces an acute painful glaucoma. The process is a phacotoxic macrophage reaction rather than an immune granulomatous response to lens antigen.
additionalDifferentials: acute anterior uveitis with secondary glaucoma
lens particle glaucoma following capsular rupture
additionalInvestigations: slit-lamp examination for hypermature cataract, pseudohypopyon and iridescent particles
B-scan ultrasonography to assess the posterior segment when the fundus is obscured
aqueous aspirate cytology showing protein-laden macrophages when the diagnosis is uncertain
corneal assessment for oedema and endothelial status before surgery
biometry of the fellow eye to aid surgical planning
redFlags: acute painful eye with very high intraocular pressure and corneal oedema
rapidly progressive optic nerve compromise from sustained pressure
signs suggesting endophthalmitis rather than sterile lens-induced inflammation
an only eye or bilateral hypermature cataracts requiring urgent intervention
reference.prognosis: Prompt cataract extraction usually normalises intraocular pressure and the glaucoma resolves without long-term medication, though final vision depends on the health of the optic nerve and macula after any period of sustained high pressure.
pitfalls: Mistaking the presentation for acute angle closure and performing iridotomy instead of addressing the lens.
Confusing the pseudohypopyon with infective endophthalmitis and delaying appropriate surgery.
Attempting prolonged medical control rather than proceeding to timely lens removal.
Underestimating capsular fragility, which increases the risk of intraoperative capsular rupture and vitreous loss.
Neglecting to counsel about guarded visual prognosis when the cataract is long-standing and the optic nerve status is unknown.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Lens and Cataract
management: Definitive treatment by prompt cataract extraction to remove the leaking hypermature lens and its liberated protein

Immediate medical intraocular pressure reduction with topical aqueous suppressants such as beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, plus systemic acetazolamide and hyperosmotic agents before surgery
Topical corticosteroids to control the associated macrophage-driven inflammation
Corneal and endothelial assessment to optimise the timing and safety of surgery when there is corneal oedema
Intraocular lens implantation at the time of cataract surgery once inflammation and pressure are controlled
Postoperative monitoring of intraocular pressure and the optic nerve, as the glaucoma usually resolves without long-term medication
Referral to an ophthalmic surgeon, with assessment and planned management of the fellow eye cataract
